html:
Since February 2009 more than 150 Tibetans, many of them monks and nuns, have set themselves on fire in protest against Chinese rule. The first was Tapey, a young monk of Kirti monastery in Ngawa, a Tibetan area of Sichuan; most of the burnings came in 2011 and 2012.

Many called out for the return of the Dalai Lama and for freedom for Tibet as they burned, and most died. The protests followed the crackdown after the unrest of 2008 across the Tibetan plateau, with tight control of monasteries, campaigns of "patriotic education" and limits on travel and on the Tibetan language. Ngawa, with Kirti monastery at its centre, was the focus.

China calls the acts terrorism, blames the Dalai Lama's followers abroad, and has jailed relatives and friends of those who burned themselves for inciting them. The Dalai Lama has neither praised nor condemned them. Their form recalls the protest of the Vietnamese monk Thich Quang Duc in 1963, during the Buddhist crisis. Tibetans in exile honour them as martyrs.
